flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that the closed backward walk must give a directed cycle of length at most 3. Pigeonhole only bounds the cycle length by 5, so this step does not follow.
counterexample: The directed 5-cycle on vertices 1..5 with arcs 1→2→3→4→5→1. It has no loops. Its only directed cycle has length 5, so it has none of length 2 or 3. Every vertex has in-degree exactly 1, so no vertex has in-degree 0.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt, with a verdict on each step:
1. Assume for contradiction that every vertex of D has in-degree at least 1. — Justified: this is the negation of the conclusion.
2. Start at any vertex v0. Repeatedly pick an in-neighbour, giving v1→v0, v2→v1, and so on. — Justified: step 1 guarantees an in-neighbour always exists.
3. Among v0..v5 there are 6 vertices from a set of 5, so some vertex repeats (vi = vj with i < j). The part of the walk between them contains a directed cycle of length between 1 and 5. Loops are excluded, so the length is between 2 and 5. — Justified: pigeonhole, and a shortest repeat gives a simple cycle.
4. That cycle therefore has length at most 3, which contradicts the hypothesis. — NOT justified: step 3 only gives length at most 5. Cycles of length 4 or 5 are allowed by the hypothesis.
5. So some vertex has in-degree 0. — Not justified, because it relies on step 4.

Testing whether the gap can be closed: the directed 5-cycle 1→2→3→4→5→1 is loopless and on exactly 5 vertices. Its only cycle has length 5, so it has no directed 2- or 3-cycle. Yet every vertex has in-degree 1. It satisfies every hypothesis but breaks the conclusion. The statement is false, and no repair of step 4 is possible.
